title: Objects in the pipeline
summary: What really flows through `|` in PowerShell, how Get-Member shows it, and the four cmdlets you use every day: Where-Object, Sort-Object, Select-Object and ForEach-Object.

steps.title: The pipe carries objects
body: In bash, `|` passes **text**: the next program gets lines of characters and has to cut the value it wants out of them
by position (`awk '{print $5}'`) or by pattern. Change the column layout and the script breaks.
In PowerShell, `|` passes **.NET objects**. `Get-ChildItem` emits `FileInfo` objects; each one *has* a `Length` (a
number), a `LastWriteTime` (a date) and a `Name`. The next cmdlet reads the property it needs by name. Nothing is
parsed, so sorting by size is numeric and comparing dates is a real date comparison.
Step through a real run below. Orange properties are the ones each command reads. `60KB` is a number literal
(61440): `KB`, `MB`, `GB` and `TB` suffixes work anywhere in PowerShell. Then compare with what bash would see.

stages.note: Six file objects come out. The table you normally see is only a *view* of them; each object has about twenty properties.
`Where-Object` reads `Length` on each object and passes on the ones where `-gt 61440` is true. `nightly.log.1` is exactly 60 KB, so it is dropped: *greater than* is strict.
Sorted as numbers, biggest first. They are still the same `FileInfo` objects: you could still call `.Delete()` on them here.
`Select-Object` builds **new** objects with only the properties you asked for, plus a *calculated* one (`KB`). From here on they are no longer files.

text: # what flows between the commands is only this text:
# awk must know the size is the 5th space-separated column, and a name with a space breaks $9.
# sort -rn has to be told the text is a number.

steps.prompt: Why does `Get-ChildItem | Sort-Object Length` sort `9 KB` before `10 KB`, while sorting the text of `ls -l` with plain `sort` puts `10240` before `9216`?
options: `Length` is a number (an `Int64`) on each object, so Sort-Object compares numbers; plain `sort` compares characters
PowerShell reads the size from the disk again while sorting
steps.explain: Sort-Object compares values by their type: numbers as numbers, dates as dates, strings as strings (case-insensitive by default). Text tools only ever see strings, which is why bash needs `sort -n`, `-k5` and friends. The flip side: if the *property* is a string (everything from `Import-Csv` is), Sort-Object sorts it as text too. The boss has that bug.

steps.title: Get-Member: what is in the box?
body: When you do not know what an object holds, pipe it to `Get-Member` (alias `gm`). It prints the **type name** and every
property and method:
```powershell
Get-ChildItem ~/logs -File | Get-Member -MemberType Property
TypeName: System.IO.FileInfo
Name              MemberType Definition
FullName          Property   string FullName {get;}
LastWriteTime     Property   datetime LastWriteTime {get;set;}
Length            Property   long Length {get;}
The table PowerShell prints by default is a **view** chosen by the type's formatting rules, not all the data. To see
every property with its value, pipe one object to `Format-List *` (or `Select-Object *`):
```powershell
Get-Item ~/logs/web/error.log | Format-List *
This is the habit that makes PowerShell easy: **ask the object** (`Get-Member`, `Format-List *`) instead of guessing
property names or searching the web.

steps.title: Find the stale files
prompt: A disk is filling up. List every file under `~/logs` and `~/data` (all subfolders) that has **not been changed for more
than 30 days**. Write their **full paths**, one per line, into `~/answers/stale.txt`.
First use `Get-Member` (or `Format-List *` on one file) to find the property that holds the full path and the one that
holds the time of the last change. `(Get-Date).AddDays(-30)` is the date 30 days ago.

checks.name: stale.txt lists exactly the old files
checks.fail: `~/answers/stale.txt` should hold the full path of each file changed more than 30 days ago (3 files), one per line. The diff shows `<` for lines that should not be there and `>` for missing ones.

checks.name: the paths are full paths
checks.fail: Write the `FullName` of each file, like `/home/learner/logs/jobs/README.txt`, not just the `Name`.

hints: `Get-ChildItem ~/logs -File | Select-Object -First 1 | Format-List *` shows every property of one file. Look for the full path and the last write time.
`Get-ChildItem ~/logs, ~/data -Recurse -File | Where-Object LastWriteTime -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-30)` keeps the old ones.
Then `| Select-Object -ExpandProperty FullName | Set-Content ~/answers/stale.txt` writes just the paths.
solution: Get-ChildItem ~/logs, ~/data -Recurse -File | Where-Object LastWriteTime -lt $cutoff | Select-Object -ExpandProperty FullName | Set-Content ~/answers/stale.txt
steps.explain: Real clean-up scripts start exactly like this, with a list you can read before anything is deleted. `-Recurse -File` walks every subfolder and skips the folder objects. In module 3 this becomes a clean-up with `-WhatIf`.

steps.title: The everyday four
body: | Cmdlet | Does | Example |
| `Where-Object` | keeps the objects where a condition is true | `Where-Object Length -gt 1MB` |
| `Sort-Object` | sorts by one or more properties | `Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending` |
| `Select-Object` | picks properties, or the first / last N objects | `Select-Object Name, Length -First 5` |
| `ForEach-Object` | runs a script block for each object | `ForEach-Object { $_.Name.ToUpper() }` |
Inside a script block, **`$_`** (also spelled `$PSItem`) is the current object. `Where-Object Length -gt 1MB` is the short
form of `Where-Object { $_.Length -gt 1MB }`; use the script block when the condition has more than one part:
`Where-Object { $_.Extension -eq '.log' -and $_.Length -gt 1MB }`.
**`-Property` or `-ExpandProperty`?** `Select-Object Name` makes new objects that *have* a Name property (shown as
`@{Name=access.log}` when turned into text). `Select-Object -ExpandProperty Name` outputs the **plain values**
(`access.log`). Use `-ExpandProperty` (or `(...).Name`) when the next step wants the value itself: a file, a log line,
another command's argument.
**Filter left.** When the first command can filter for you, let it: `Get-ChildItem -Filter *.log` asks the file system
for only those names, which is far faster on a big share than `Get-ChildItem | Where-Object Name -like '*.log'`.

steps.explain: `1..6` is a range: the numbers 1 to 6, sent down the pipe one at a time. `Where-Object` keeps the even ones, `ForEach-Object` multiplies each by 10, and each result is printed on its own line.

steps.prompt: This writes `@{Name=access.log}` lines into the file instead of plain names. Which change fixes it?
steps.explain: `Select-Object Name` makes objects with one property; `Set-Content` turns each object into text with `.ToString()`, which for those objects is `@{Name=...}`. `-ExpandProperty` sends the string values themselves.

steps.prompt: Build the pipeline: the names of the five biggest `.csv` files under `~/data`, biggest first.
steps.explain: Filter first (`-Filter` at the source), sort, take the top five, then turn the objects into the plain names. A line that ends with `|` continues on the next line, so long pipelines stay readable.

steps.title: The five biggest files
prompt: Before anyone buys more disk, find where the space went. Write the **names** (not paths) of the **five biggest files**
anywhere under `~/data`, biggest first, one per line, into `~/answers/top5.txt`.
Look at the sizes first: `Get-ChildItem ~/data -Recurse -File | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object Name, Length`.

checks.name: top5.txt has the five biggest names, biggest first
checks.cmd: diff <(tr -d '\r' < ~/answers/top5.txt | sed '/^$/d') <(find ~/data -type f -printf '%s %f\n' | sort -rn | head -n5 | cut -d' ' -f2)
checks.fail: `~/answers/top5.txt` should hold exactly five file names, biggest first. The diff shows what differs (`>` is what should be there).

hints: `-Recurse -File` walks all subfolders and returns only files.
`Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 5` gives the five biggest objects.
solution: Get-ChildItem ~/data -Recurse -File | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object Name, Length -First 8
Get-ChildItem ~/data -Recurse -File | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 -ExpandProperty Name | Set-Content ~/answers/top5.txt
steps.explain: On a Windows file server the same line answers "what filled the D: drive?". Add `@{ n = 'GB'; e = { [math]::Round($_.Length / 1GB, 2) } }` to the `Select-Object` for a readable report; the next lesson shows how.
